items.q: A 28‑year‑old baseball pitcher presents with pain and loss of active flexion at the proximal interphalangeal joint of his index finger. MRI shows absence of the central slip of the distal interphalangeal joint extension apparatus. Which extensor tendon component is most likely injured?
o: Lateral band of the DIP tendon
items.e: Damage to the central slip of the extensor digitorum communis adjacent to the middle phalanx produces a classic “swan‑neck” deformity with extension lag at the PIP joint.

items.q: In a patient with acute wrist trauma, which finding at 8 weeks post‑fracture most strongly suggests the need for surgical exploration of a neurovascular structure?
o: Painful pillar sensation resolving after compression
items.e: An acute wrist fracture that results in persistent motor deficit (e.g., wrist drop) indicates probable nerve injury that requires surgery; medical management alone is insufficient.

items.q: A healthy 28‑year‑old man sustains a closed fracture of the distal radius. Which of the following statements about the likelihood of radial nerve injury is correct?
o: All such fractures cause axonotmesis of the radial nerve
Only fractures involving the lunate facet are associated with radial nerve palsy
Observation and serial EMG are adequate if no recovery by 4–6 months
Radial nerve palsy in these fractures is always permanent
items.e: Closed distal radius fractures usually cause neurapraxia/axonotmesis; if there is no clinical recovery by 3–6 months, EMG should be repeated and surgical exploration considered.

items.q: In a patient undergoing an elbow flexion nerve transfer using the Oberlin technique, the surgeon chooses a fascicle of the ulnar nerve to anastomose to the biceps motor branch. Which postoperative finding would best confirm successful reinnervation?
o: Recovery of wrist drop within 2 weeks
Return of elbow flexion strength at 3 months
Resumption of sensory function in the medial forearm
Development of a claw hand posture
items.e: Myoelectric and clinical recovery of elbow flexion at about 3 months is the typical yardstick for Oberlin transfer success.

items.q: A 45‑year‑old woman had a first‑rib fracture after a motor vehicle collision. Six weeks later she develops weakness of the intrinsic hand muscles and a claw hand deformity. What is the most appropriate investigation to distinguish between a root avulsion and a post‑ganglionic rupture?
items.e: EMG/NCV will show denervation changes and absence of SNAPs in root avulsion, whereas post‑ganglionic lesions retain SNAPs.

items.q: A patient presents with a 3‑mm widening of the scapholunate interval on a PA wrist view and the scaphoid is found to be flexed while the lunate is extended. Which of the following statements is FALSE regarding this injury?
o: The scaphoid flexes and the lunate extends
A gap over about 3 mm on the PA view suggests scapholunate dissociation
The scapholunate angle is increased above 60°
items.e: VISI (volar intercalated segment instability) follows lunotriquetral injury, not scapholunate dissociation.
items.reason: Repeats b938 (FALSE statement about scapholunate dissociation)

items.q: A 25‑year‑old sprinter falls onto an outstretched hand. X‑ray shows a displaced waist fracture of the scaphoid with a humpback angle of 38° on sagittal CT. Which treatment is most appropriate?
o: Percutaneous headless screw fixation via a volar approach
Open reduction with a volar wedge cortical‑cancellous graft and screw
Open reduction via a dorsal approach with a 1,2‑ICSRA vascularized graft
items.e: Displaced waist fractures with humpback deformity demand open reduction and grafting; a volar wedge graft restores the scaphoid’s curvature.

items.q: The imaging modality that provides the highest sensitivity and specificity for detecting an occult scaphoid fracture within the first week of injury is
items.e: Early MRI (within days of injury) detects occult fractures with near‑100 % sensitivity and specificity.
items.reason: Repeats b324 (MRI for occult scaphoid fracture)

items.q: According to the Herbert classification, a complete waist fracture that is unstable but without comminution falls into which category?
items.e: B2 denotes an unstable, complete waist fracture.

items.q: A 5‑year‑old child presents with a partial duplication of the thumb that appears bifid at the distal phalanx level. Which Wassel type does this represent?
items.e: The description matches Wassel type I, which is a bifid distal phalanx. Types II–IV involve duplication at higher levels.

items.q: During the phased release of simple syndactyly involving the third webspace, which of the following is the recommended age for intervention to avoid angular deformity?
items.e: Release of the third webspace is best done at 6–12 months; earlier release allows correction before the longer finger causes tethering.

items.q: Which signalling centre in limb development, when duplicated, is responsible for ulnar dimelia (mirror hand)?
items.e: Duplication of the ZPA leads to sonic hedgehog (SHH) over‑expression, producing mirror hand (ulnar dimelia).

items.q: A child presents with a short, polydactylous hand that also shows clinodactyly of the middle finger and a hypoplastic thumb. Which HOX gene mutation is most likely implicated?
items.e: HOXD13 mutations are associated with synpolydactyly, characterized by digit duplication plus clinodactyly and thumb hypoplasia.

items.q: What classification is used to stage the total flexion deformity of Dupuytren’s disease on a per‑ray basis?
items.e: The Tubiana classification grades the deformity per ray from 0 (no deformity) to stage 4 (over 135°).

items.q: A 32‑year‑old woman presents with a painful hallux valgus, HVA 22° and IMA 15°. She has mild dorsal subluxation of the proximal phalanx on the metatarsal head (incongruent joint). Which osteotomy should be performed to correct the angular deformity without creating an iatrogenic incongruity?
items.e: B. A biplanar chevron osteotomy corrects both the HVA and the increased DMAA seen in incongruent joints while preserving congruency; a simple distal chevron would leave the DMAA unaddressed.

items.q: A 47‑year‑old patient has Hallux Valgus angle 38°, IMA 18°, and a documented first‑tarsometatarsal joint hypermobility (dorsal translation >8 mm) on standing AP radiograph. The operative procedure that simultaneously corrects the IMA and stabilises the first TMT joint is:

items.q: Which of the following is ANIMALITICALLY FAILING to prevent recurrence of hallux valgus after a chevron osteotomy?

items.e: B. If the DMAA is raised, residual joint incongruity will recur; a simple chevron without correcting DMAA leaves the deformity unaddressed.

items.q: A 60‑year‑old diabetic woman with motor‑sensory loss presents with a painful hallux valgus (HVA 41°, IMA 21°) and a shaft‑lengthened first metatarsal. Which surgical option provides the best chance of pain relief while avoiding transfer metatarsalgia?
o: Scarf osteotomy with L-shaped opening wedge
Proximal chevron with repositioned metatarsal head
items.e: D. Arthrodesis offloads the painful joint and eliminates the shaft‑lengthened metatarsal’s load‑bearing problem; osteotomies risk shortening or dorsal malunion.

items.q: During a percutaneous chevron osteotomy, the surgeon inadvertently over‑releases the lateral capsule, resulting in a sudden increase in HVA by 10°. The most appropriate immediate corrective step is:
o: Primary insertion of a lateral capsule graft
Re‑position and fixation of the distally displaced metatarsal head with a full‑thickness cartilage graft

items.q: Which of the following statements best describes the relationship between the first‑tarsometatarsal joint and severe hallux valgus?

First‑TMT hypermobility is found in up to 80% of patients with IMA >16°
Unstable first TMT requires a Salter‑Galeazzi osteotomy for correction

items.e: B. Studies report first‑TMT instability in around 80 % of severe cases; this instability perpetuates the IMA and thus necessitates arthrodesis if present.

items.q: During correction of a flexible adult flatfoot, a medializing displacement calcaneal osteotomy is performed. Which complication is most likely if the osteotomy gap is over‑filled with bone graft?
items.e: Over‑grafting creates excessive lateral column tension, resulting in lateral foot pain— the most common iatrogenic problem after a MDCO.

items.q: Which of the following is the best non‑operative treatment for a fibrous rupture of the tibialis posterior tendon in an elderly low‑demand patient?
items.e: A short‑leg cast or removable orthosis is the standard first‑line approach; steroids risk tendon rupture and transfers or tenonisation are surgical interventions.

items.q: In a patient with a rigid adult flatfoot (fixed hindfoot valgus) and tibiotalar arthritis, the most suitable operative procedure is:
items.e: When the deformity is rigid and the ankle is arthritic, a tibiotalocalcaneal (TTC) arthrodesis addresses both the hindfoot malalignment and the tibiotalar arthritis in one operation.

items.q: A 35‑year‑old recreational jogger hears a pop in the back of his right leg while running and immediately feels a loss of push‑off. In the clinic his calf squeeze test is negative, but a gap is palpable. Which investigation best determines the extent of the rupture and guides treatment?
items.e: Dynamic ultrasound visualises the gap, its size in plantarflexion and whether the ends appose, thereby directing operative versus functional management.

items.q: The most common site of spontaneous Achilles rupture is 2–6 cm above the insertion. What anatomical feature makes this region most susceptible?

items.q: During a physical exam a patient presents with a sudden sensation of “being kicked in the back of the leg” and performs a calf squeeze test that shows plantarflexion. Which statement about this scenario is FALSE?
o: The tendon rupture is most likely acute

items.q: An athlete reports pain at the back of the heel with activity that improves with rest and has a small swelling that moves with the tendon. Which of the following diagnoses is most likely in a 11‑year‑old?
items.e: Sever disease is traction apophysitis of the calcaneal ossification centre in children, presenting with activity‑related heel pain that resolves with rest.

items.q: Which of the following statements about Achilles tendinopathy treatment is correct?
o: A large‑volume corticosteroid injection into the tendon is first‑line therapy
Eccentric loading is recommended for the mid‑portion subtype
ESWT is only indicated for insertional disease
Heavy‑weight resistance is contraindicated in the early phase
items.e: Eccentric loading (Alfredson protocol) is the established first‑line treatment for mid‑portion Achilles tendinopathy; corticosteroid injections are contraindicated as they can precipitate rupture.

items.q: A 45‑year‑old man presents with dull ankle pain for 6 months, swelling, and a 10 ° increase in the ankle joint space on an AP radiograph. He had a twisting injury 4 years ago. Which investigation is the most appropriate next step to confirm post‑traumatic ankle arthritis?
items.e: Post‑traumatic ankle arthritis is best confirmed with a weight‑bearing ankle axial (or mortise) view; it shows joint space narrowing and subchondral sclerosis.

items.q: In a modified Broström‑Gould repair for a chronic ATFL tear, which additional structure is typically used for reinforcement?
items.e: The Gould modification uses the inferior extensor retinaculum to reinforce the repaired ATFL and CFL.
items.reason: Repeats cai20261107_014 (Gould modification of Broström)

items.q: A 30‑year‑old athlete had a severe inversion sprain with ATFL and CFL tears. In the acute setting, which functional treatment is most evidence‑based for early mobilization?
o: An ankle‑brace with early weight bearing
Immediate surgical repair of ATFL and CFL
items.e: Functional treatment with a brace and early mobilization is superior to immobilisation for most acute sprains; short cast/boot only helps grade III injuries.

items.q: A 28‑year‑old man presents 5 days after a motor‑vehicle collision with a displaced talar neck fracture. X‑ray shows a posterior subtalar dislocation. Which statement best explains the risk of avascular necrosis in this injury?
o: AVN risk is low because the talar body is still vascularised by the tarsal canal artery
AVN risk is high because the deltoid ligament is often torn, compromising the deltoid branch
AVN risk is high due to disruption of the intraosseous blood supply in the talar neck
AVN risk is negligible if the fracture is reduced within 24 hours
items.e: The talar neck receives its blood supply mainly from intraosseous vessels; a displaced fracture severing these vessels predisposes to avascular necrosis.

items.q: A 32‑year‑old woman sustains a lateral process fracture of the talus (snowboarder’s fracture). Surgical treatment is indicated if:
o: Fracture is only a hairline crack with no displacement
Fracture is more than 1 cm in width or displaced
The patient is a professional athlete
The fracture is intra‑articular and involves the talonavicular joint
items.e: Displacement >1 cm or significant width warrants ORIF; small, undisplaced fractures are managed non‑operatively.

items.q: Which of the following statements about the medial talar process (Cedell fracture) is correct?
o: It is caused by forced plantarflexion followed by severe dorsal flexion
It results from pronation‑dorsiflexion forces producing an avulsion of the posterior tibiotalar deltoid
It is usually treated with open reduction and internal fixation via a lateral approach
It is synonymous with the lateral tubercle (Shepherd) fracture
items.e: Cedell fractures arise from pronation‑dorsiflexion and involve an avulsion of the posterior deltoid matrix.

items.q: A 45‑year‑old man is suspected of having an intra‑articular calcaneal fracture involving the posterior facet. Which imaging view is most valuable for confirming the fracture line?
items.e: The Canale view best visualises the talar neck and adjacent facets; it is essential for detecting posterior‑facet fractures.

items.q: After fixation of a type I talar neck fracture (undisplaced), which of the following post‑operative instructions is evidence‑based?
o: Immediate full weight‑bearing in a rigid cast for 12 weeks
Weight‑bearing as tolerated from day one
Use of a functional brace with early ankle mobilisation for 4 weeks
items.e: Undisplaced fractures are best managed with a 6–12‑week non‑weight‑bearing cast; early mobilisation is acceptable only in selected cases.

items.q:
A 28‑year‑old hand‑stand gymnast presents with a sudden inability to flex the index finger while tapering off a handball. The gap is found over the middle phalanx and ultrasound confirms a ruptured tendon. Which tendon is almost certainly involved?
A) FDP of the index finger
B) FDS of the index finger
C) FDP of the middle finger
D) FDS of the middle finger
items.e: The FDP of the index finger has a separate muscle belly and therefore acts independently of the other fingers’ FDPs; it is the most common isolated flexor tendon injured.

items.q:

B) Hunter‑type reconstruction
C) Sydney‑type reconstruction

items.e: Hunter’s two‑stage flexor tendon reconstruction involves placing a silicone rod to form a pseudosheath first, then grafting the tendon later once the sheath is mature.

items.q: A 32‑year‑old man presents with numbness in the first three digits of the hand and a weak key pinch. On examination, a Tinel sign is positive at the wrist. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Median nerve compression at the wrist (Carpal Tunnel Syndrome)
Ulnar nerve entrapment at the elbow
items.e: The classic sensory distribution and positive Tinel sign localise the lesion to the median nerve in the carpal tunnel.

items.q: In which of the following situations is a Tinel sign most likely to advance during recovery?
o: Endoneurial irritation of the median nerve
items.e: An advancing Tinel sign is characteristic of axonotmesis (Sunderland stage II) where axons regenerate along intact fascicles.

items.q: A patient with a history of rheumatic arthritis develops sudden loss of key pinch and a painful “ape‑thumb deformity”. Which of the following interventions is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
o: Hand‑wrist immobilisation in a dorsal splint for 6 weeks
Corticosteroid injection into the carpal tunnel
items.e: Severe median nerve compression with functional loss warrants prompt surgical decompression.

items.q: A 28‑year‑old pharmacist presents with burning pain over the dorsoradial aspect of the hand triggered by forearm pronation. Electromyography shows no motor weakness. Which nerve is most likely compressed?
items.e: The described sensory distribution and lack of motor symptoms point to Wartenberg’s syndrome, compression of the superficial radial nerve.

items.q: A 25‑year‑old cyclist presents with shoulder abduction and external rotation weakness, elbow flexion intact, and a prominent winged scapula. Examination shows pain on resisted forward elevation. Which nerve is most likely injured?
items.e: The patient’s presentation—loss of abduction/external rotation with a winged scapula—represents Erb’s palsy, classically due to upper trunk injury. The axillary nerve, arising from the posterior cord (C5‑6), supplies the deltoid and teres minor; its palsy results in the described deficits.

items.q: A 30‑year‑old man sustains a motorcycle crash. He has a T1 level root avulsion. Six weeks later he complains of constant burning pain in the left arm, unaffected muscle bulk but absent sensation over the lateral forearm. Which surgical intervention is most appropriate for pain relief?
o: Spinal accessory to suprascapular nerve transfer
items.e: Root avulsion produces longstanding deafferentation pain. DREZ ablation selectively disrupts hyperactive dorsal horn neurons and is the preferred technique for severe, medication‑resistant neuropathic pain after pre‑ganglionic injury.

items.q: A 45‑year‑old woman presents with a painless, flail limb after a fall on an outstretched arm. Neurological exam reveals a 2‑cm pseudomeningocele at the C6 root on MRI. Which investigation would best confirm the nature of the lesion?
o: CT myelography of the cervical spine
items.e: CT myelography is most sensitive for detecting rootlet avulsion and pseudomeningoceles, allowing differentiation between pre‑ and post‑ganglionic injuries.

items.q: An adolescent boy with a high‑energy trauma to the shoulder has loss of elbow flexion and weakened wrist supination. Neurology reveals preserved forearm sensation. Which nerve transfer is the most logical first step in reconstruction?
o: Oberlin transfer (ulnar fascicle to biceps motor branch)
items.e: Elbow flexion is a priority in brachial plexus reconstruction; the Oberlin transfer uses a single fascicle of the ulnar nerve to reinnervate the biceps, providing early elbow flexion while preserving ulnar function.

items.q: A 60‑year‑old retired sailor has a chronic pan‑plexus injury with lost shoulder abduction, elbow flexion, and intrinsic hand function. After 18 months, he presents for definitive surgery. Which free‑muscle transfer is most appropriate for restoring elbow flexion?
o: Gracilis to biceps with spinal accessory neurotisation
Latissimus dorsi to biceps with intercostal nerve graft
Posterior interosseous nerve to biceps with contralateral C7 graft
Gastrocnemius to biceps with ulnar nerve graft
items.e: In late pan‑plexus cases, a gracilis free‑muscle transfer reinnervated by the spinal accessory nerve provides reliable elbow flexion, with the donor muscle being expendable and the neurotisation pathway often intact.

items.q: A 25‑year‑old male falls on an outstretched hand. X‑rays of the wrist are normal, but he continues to have pain over the anatomical snuffbox. Which investigation is most appropriate to rule out a subtle scaphoid fracture?
o: CT scan with axial cuts of the scaphoid
MRI taken within the first 48 hours
Repeat PA wrist radiograph after 4 weeks
items.e: Early MRI has near‑100 % sensitivity and specificity for occult scaphoid fractures and avoids unnecessary immobilisation.

items.q: An 18‑year‑old presents with a displaced waist fracture of the scaphoid measuring 1.5 mm on CT. What is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Dorsal open reduction and internal fixation
Volar wrist arthroscopy with graft placement
items.e: A displacement >1 mm constitutes an unstable fracture; percutaneous fixation is preferred to achieve early union.

items.q: Which of the following falls under the ‘B’ group in the Herbert classification of scaphoid fractures?
items.e: B‑category fractures are unstable acute fractures; B3 denotes a proximal pole fracture.

items.q: A patient with a chronic, displaced scaphoid non‑union develops a pronounced humpback deformity. Which surgical option is most appropriate?
o: Percutaneous screw fixation with bone graft
Volar inlay cancellous graft and screw fixation
items.e: Humpback deformity requires open reduction, a volar wedge cancellous graft (Fisk‑Fernandez) and screw fixation.

items.q: The normal range for the scapholunate angle on a lateral wrist radiograph is:
items.e: Normal scapholunate angles fall between 30–60° (mean ≈47°).

items.q: A 32‑year‑old construction worker presents with a tender, swollen pulp of the right index finger after sustaining a splinter injury. Examination shows a tense, fluctuant swelling restricted to the distal phalanx region. Which incision is most appropriate for drainage?
o: Ulnar-lateral (mid‑axial) incision along the non‑contact side
Volar longitudinal incision across the dorsal interdigital space
Radial-lateral incision across the dorsal web space
Transverse incision over the proximal interphalangeal joint
items.e: The closed‑space infection (felon) is best drained through a high‑lateral mid‑axial incision on the non‑contact (ulnar) side of the index finger; this approach avoids the neurovascular bundles, flexor sheath and preserves a cosmetically acceptable scar.

items.q: A 45‑year‑old diabetic patient develops painful swelling of the thenar eminence on the right hand. Physical exam reveals an abducted thumb with a widened first web space. The infection is confined to the thenar space. What is the recommended dual‑incision approach for adequate drainage?
o: Volar incision along the thenar crease and a dorsal incision over the first web space
Single volar longitudinal incision from wrist to thumb
Dorsal incision over the first web with a small palmar stab
Single dorsal incision over the thumb with a wide flared edge
items.e: The thenar space lies deep to the index flexor tendon and superficial to the adductor pollicis; thus, a volar incision along the thenar crease (avoiding the recurrent branch) combined with a dorsal longitudinal incision over the first web is the standard dual‑incision technique.

items.q: A 27‑year‑old firefighter presents with a sudden, throbbing pain at the tip of his left little finger after inhaling hot vapors. Examination shows a clear, clustered vesicular eruption on an erythematous base, with the pulp non‑tense. Which statement best guides management?
o: Incise the vesicles to drain the fluid and apply a sterile dressing
Apply a protective dressing and consider oral acyclovir if within 48 h
Perform a Tzanck smear before initiating any treatment
items.e: Herpetic whitlow is a self‑limited HSV infection; incising vesicles risks secondary bacterial infection and systemic viraemia. A protective dressing plus early oral acyclovir (within 48–72 h) is the preferred non‑operative approach.

items.q: A 5‑year‑old boy with a history of Type 2 diabetes presents with a painful, swollen right ring finger. No clear puncture wound is noted. Examination shows a fusiform swelling of the digit, tenderness along the flexor tendon sheath, and pain on passive extension. What is the most appropriate initial management for this suspected condition?
o: Immediate broad‑spectrum intravenous antibiotics and splint in the safe position
Early surgical drainage with a single incision at the A1 pulley
Start oral clindamycin and observe for 48 h
Administer intramuscular dexamethasone to reduce swelling
items.e: The presentation is classic for pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis. Early IV antibiotics plus splinting in the safe position are indicated if the infection is equivocal; reassess within 12–24 h before proceeding to surgical drainage.

items.q: Which organism is least likely to be the culprit in a community‑acquired hand infection following a simple finger prick?
items.e: Community‑acquired hand infections usually involve S. aureus (often MRSA), beta‑haemolytic streptococci, or mixed anaerobes in bites. Mycobacterium marinum is associated with chronic fish‑tank related infections, not a simple prick.

items.q: Which of the following best describes the embryological signalling centre responsible for radial‑ulnar patterning of the upper limb?
items.e: The zone of polarising activity (ZPA) located in the posterior mesoderm secretes Sonic hedgehog and dictates the anterior‑posterior (radial‑ulnar) axis. Disruptions lead to mirror hand or radial/ulnar deficiencies.

items.q: Which of the following complications is most common following release of central‑digit syndactyly when a split‑thickness graft is used?
items.e: Web creep, defined as distal migration of the new web, is the most frequent problem with split‑thickness grafts used in syndactyly repair.

items.q: A 2‑year‑old child is diagnosed with postaxial type B polydactyly of the fifth finger. At what age is surgical removal typically performed?
items.e: Type B ulnar polydactyly (rudimentary nubbin) is usually excised between 9 and 12 months to allow adequate soft‑tissue maturity while minimizing scarring.

items.q: A 55‑year‑old woman with a long history of rheumatoid arthritis has a sudden inability to extend her little finger on the left hand. Examination reveals a tender swelling at the dorsal distal ulna. Which tendon is most likely ruptured?
o: Extensor digitorum profundus of the ring finger
items.e: In rheumatoid arthritic hands, attrition over a eroded distal ulna preferentially tears the dorsalmost extensor tendons – the extensor digiti minimi (EDM) – manifesting first as a little‑finger extension loss.

items.q: A 35‑year‑old woman presents with a 22° hallux valgus angle and a 15° intermetatarsal angle on weight‑bearing AP radiographs. The first tarsometatarsal joint is clinically found to be hypermobile. Which operation will correct the deformity while stabilising the first TMT joint?
items.e: A distal chevron targets mild to moderate deformities; a 15° IMA needs a proximal correction. Fusing the first TMT joint (modified Lapidus) corrects the IMA at its apex and stabilises the joint.

items.q: Which of the following is the most common complication after a distal chevron osteotomy performed without protecting the nutrient vessels of the first metatarsal?

items.q: In a patient with a severe hallux valgus (HVA >40°, IMA >20°) and mild first MTP joint arthritis, the surgeon chooses a proximal metatarsal osteotomy plus a distal soft‑tissue release. Which complication is most likely if the osteotomy is a closing‑wedge with excessive dorsally directed osteotomy blade?

Joint stiffness unrelated to the osteotomy
Infection at the base of the first metatarsal

items.q: A 68‑year‑old obese woman presents with medial ankle pain that worsens when she attempts a single‑leg heel‑rise; the heel does not invert. Which tendon is most likely dysfunctional?
items.e: Impaired inversion on heel rise is the classic sensitive test for posterior tibial tendon dysfunction, the main dynamic stabiliser of the medial arch.

items.q: On a weight‑bearing lateral foot radiograph the Meary angle (talo‑first metatarsal angle) is 12° convex toward the plantar surface. Which statement is true?
items.e: A Meary angle of 4°–15° is considered mild flatfoot; angles >15° signify moderate disease and might warrant operative correction.

items.q: In middle‑aged obese women, which factor is most frequently implicated as the initiating lesion in adult acquired flatfoot?
items.e: Degeneration of the tibialis posterior tendon is the classic and most common initiating event, especially in obese women, before spring‑ligament failure becomes apparent.

items.q: Which investigation is the investigation of choice for detecting tears or tendinosis of the tibialis posterior tendon in suspected adult acquired flatfoot?
items.e: MRI provides direct visualization of tendon integrity, flow voids, and inflammatory changes, making it the gold standard for TP tendon assessment.

items.q: A 34‑year‑old male presents with sudden pain at the back of the right leg while running, reports hearing a pop. On examination the calf squeeze (Thompson) test is negative and he can still plantarflex. Which statement about this presentation is correct?

The resting ankle should always be in dorsiflexion during repair

items.q: Which imaging modality is best for determining the gap size in a suspected acute Achilles rupture that will guide the decision between functional rehabilitation and operative repair?

CT scan of the lower leg

o: V‑Y lengthening of the gastrocnemius aponeurosis + FHL transfer
Tenodesis of the FDL to the calcaneus
items.e: A 3–6 cm gap (Kuwada class III) is best addressed by a gastrocnemius V‑Y lengthening with or without an FHL transfer. End‑to‑end repair is reserved for gaps <3 cm.

items.e: Percutaneous techniques carry a 5–10 % risk of sural nerve injury because the nerve crosses lateral to the tendon ~10 cm proximal to the insertion.

items.q: During the assessment of a diabetic foot ulcer, the clinician performs a probe‑to‑bone test that returns a positive result. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: A positive probe‑to‑bone test has a high predictive value for osteomyelitis in high‑prevalence settings, indicating infection of bone.

items.q: A diabetic patient with a plantar forefoot ulcer has an ABI of 1.35 but TcPO₂ at the dorsum of the toe measures 25 mmHg. What does this suggest?
o: Peripheral arterial disease is adequately managed
The ABI is falsely high due to medial calcification
The toe has adequate perfusion for healing
items.e: A high ABI (>1.3) can be falsely reassuring because of calcification; low toe pressure or TcPO₂ indicates true ischemia that would impair healing.

items.q: Which of the following is the gold standard for diagnosing osteomyelitis in a diabetic foot ulcer?
o: Bone biopsy with culture and histology
items.e: A bone biopsy (histology + culture) is the definitive test; MRI and radiographs support the diagnosis but are not definitive alone.

items.q: A 65‑year‑old diabetic presents with a painless, warm, swollen foot and radiographs showing joint fragmentation but normal ESR and CRP. Which condition is most likely?
items.e: Charcot foot presents with warmth and swelling but without systemic inflammation; normal ESR/CRP helps differentiate it from infection.

items.q: What is the most appropriate offloading technique for an uncomplicated neuropathic ulcer on the plantar surface of the forefoot?
items.e: The gold‑standard for neuropathic plantar ulcers is a non‑removable total contact cast, as it forces compliance and distributes pressure evenly.

items.q: A 45‑year‑old runner presents with dull ankle pain that worsens after repeated ankle sprains. X‑ray shows a narrowing of the tibiotalar joint space, slight osteophyte formation on the talar dome, and a decrease in Böhler angle to 25°. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: The radiographic findings—tibiotalar joint space narrowing, osteophytes, and a reduced Böhler angle—are classic for post‑traumatic ankle osteoarthritis, which constitutes 70–80% of ankle arthritic cases.

items.q: A patient with a chronic grade‑III lateral ankle sprain undergoes a Broström‑Gould repair. What postoperative complication is most frequently encountered?
o: Stiffness due to loss of inversion
items.e: Superficial peroneal nerve injury is the most common complication after Broström‑Gould procedures, reflecting the close proximity of the nerve to the operative field.

items.q: Which of the following best describes the typical sequence of ligamentous failure in an inversion‑plantarflexion ankle sprain?
items.e: The ATFL is the weakest and taut in plantarflexion, so it usually tears first, followed by the CFL, while the PTFL is rarely injured.

items.q: A patient with chronic ankle instability refuses surgery. The physiotherapist recommends a proprioceptive training programme that includes balance board exercises. This recommendation is based on evidence that:
o: Surgical repair has no added benefit over brace wear
The Broström‑Gould repair is reserved only for elite athletes
items.e: Clinical studies show that proprioceptive and peroneal strengthening can restore dynamic stability and reduce recurrent instability in many patients, making it a first‑line non‑operative treatment.

items.q: Which of the following is an indication for surgical intervention in a patient with chronic lateral ankle instability?
o: Positive anterior drawer test with more than 10 mm anterior translation
Positive talar tilt test but normal ankle ROM
Only an isolated functional giving‑way sensation
No concomitant intra‑articular lesions on arthroscopy
items.e: A positive anterior drawer test exceeding 10 mm absolute anterior translation is a mechanical sign of instability warranting anatomic repair like the Broström‑Gould procedure.

items.q: A 48‑year‑old man presents with sudden foot pain after a high‑speed motorcycle crash. X‑rays show an avulsed fragment from the lateral tubercle of the calcaneus, with no displacement of the main heel bone. What is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Immediate open reduction and internal fixation
Closed reduction under anesthesia followed by a short leg cast
Excision of the fragment with physiotherapy
items.e: Lateral tubercle (Shepherd) fractures are typically nondisplaced with a small fragment; a short‑leg cast keeps the heel stable and allows fracture healing.

items.q: Which imaging modality is essential to confirm a suspected talar neck fracture and to assess comminution?
